body:
We make Kiron, so weigh this accordingly. Everything here about the other apps comes from their App Store listings, their own help and pricing pages and independent reviews, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

Workout apps are usually compared feature by feature, but one question sorts them faster: who writes the plan? Some apps record a plan you wrote yourself. Some make up a new workout each time you open them. Some hand you a coach's program. And Kiron (that's us) runs whichever plan you choose: a ready-made one, one built from your answers, or the one you already have.

Below are eight apps grouped by who writes the plan, with prices checked November 15, 2026, and links to our longer comparisons.

If you only read this part

  • You want a plan run for you, whoever writes it: Kiron. Pick one of {{kiron:program-count}} ready-made programs, answer a few questions, or bring your own plan, and your runs go on the same calendar as your lifting.
  • You write your own routine and just want to log it: Hevy or Strong.
  • You want the app to make up each workout: Fitbod, or Hevy Trainer on Hevy's paid plan.
  • You want one coach's or author's program: Boostcamp for a big library, StrongLifts for one beginner barbell program, Ladder for a coach and a team.
  • Running comes first and lifting second: Runna.

Bottom line: pick by who writes the plan, then rule apps out on price, runs and your phone or watch. If you're not sure who should write it, Kiron covers all three ways: ready-made, built for you, or your own.

Any plan you choose, run for you: Kiron

Kiron is a workout app for {{kiron:cell-platforms}} built for the job in this guide's title. The plan can come from anywhere:

  • Pick one of {{kiron:program-count}} ready-made programs by goal: strength, muscle, your first month in a gym, home workouts with little equipment, running from a first 5K to a marathon, or lifting and cardio together. One example is the 7-Day Longevity Protocol: 16 weeks of three lifting days, a tempo run, air-bike sprints and a long easy run each week, switching between moderate and heavy weights every four weeks.
  • Answer a few questions and Kiron builds a program for you.
  • Bring the plan you already have. Paste it from ChatGPT, a coach or a website, or take a photo, and Kiron turns it into a program with sets, reps and rest, even one that changes every few weeks. A PDF goes in as pasted text or a screenshot.

Then Kiron runs it:

  • Your next workout is ready when you open the app. Train on fixed days, and Kiron can move a missed workout to your next free day. Or train whenever you get to the gym, and nothing ever counts as missed.
  • Every weight is worked out, even on day one: from your history, a related lift you've logged, or a safe standard, with a short note saying why and a "How did it feel?" check after your sets.
  • Weights go up as you get stronger, and Kiron says why it added them.
  • The plan bends without breaking. Shorten today's workout, switch to a hotel gym's equipment, or add core work or a cardio finisher in a few taps. Main lifts stay put while smaller exercises can change week to week.
  • Runs, rides, swims and rows share the calendar with your lifting, and recovery counts the workouts other apps save to Apple Health or Health Connect.
  • {{kiron:offline-lead}} {{kiron:offline-detail}}
  • Your history comes along. Kiron imports what you've logged in Fitbod, Strong or Hevy (here's how to export it) and starts your weights from it.

{{kiron:pricing-sentence}}

Where it falls short: there's no Watch app (heart rate comes from Apple Health or Health Connect after a workout), runs don't show pace, there's no social feed or export, and it's new, with a small user base. If your plan came from a chatbot, here's how to check a ChatGPT workout plan before you start.

You write the plan, the app logs it: Hevy and Strong

Hevy and Strong are workout logs. You write routines (a routine is one saved workout, such as "Push day"), and the app records every set and charts your progress. Neither builds running plans, and a plan you already have goes in by hand, one routine per workout, though Hevy's ChatGPT app can also create a plan in Hevy.

  • Hevy adds a social feed for following friends, apps for Apple Watch and Android watches, and a web version. Its free version holds 4 routines. Pro, at $23.99 a year or $74.99 once, removes the limits and adds Hevy Trainer (below). More in Hevy vs Kiron.
  • Strong is a fast, plain log with an Apple Watch app. Its free version holds 3 routines, and Pro is $29.99 a year or $99.99 once. More in our look at Strong and its alternatives.

The app makes up each workout: Fitbod and Hevy Trainer

Fitbod builds each session fresh from your history, your equipment and which muscles have recovered, and has apps for Apple Watch and Android watches. There's no free plan: after 7 days free, it's $15.99 a month or $95.99 a year for new subscribers. If you have a plan of your own, the catch is that choosing is Fitbod's job: its help center says your edits to a suggested workout are replaced if it refreshes before you start. See Fitbod vs Kiron.

Hevy Trainer comes with Hevy Pro, at $23.99 a year. It builds a lifting program from your goals, experience, equipment and schedule, and tells you when to add weight.

Both suit someone who'd rather not plan at all.

A coach or author writes it: Boostcamp, StrongLifts and Ladder

Boostcamp is a library of programs written by coaches, with a tracker. Its free tier includes 99 of its 132 coach-made programs, plus a web builder for your own that can import a spreadsheet. Pro is $59.99 a year. It has no Apple Watch app, and it's built around strength rather than cardio.

StrongLifts runs one program, a beginner barbell 5×5, and works out your weight increases and lighter weeks for you. Its support pages say it became subscription-only in 2025: it's $59.99 a year or $11.99 a month, with a 7-day trial on the yearly plan, and it has an Apple Watch app. See what changed at StrongLifts.

Ladder puts you on one of 23 teams, each led by a coach who writes a new week of workouts every Sunday, with video demos and audio coaching. Pro is $29.99 a month or $179.99 a year, the 7-day trial doesn't ask for payment details, and there's no Android app. You also need a connection to start and finish a workout. See Ladder vs Kiron.

A running app writes it: Runna

Runna is a running coach in an app. It builds plans from 5K to ultra, with pace targets that adapt as you go, and sends workouts to Apple Watch, Garmin and COROS watches. You can add strength sessions, but they're pre-built for runners, and you can't swap exercises or write your own. It's $19.99 a month or $119.99 a year. If your race comes first and lifting is support work, Runna fits; if the lifting matters as much, read whether Runna's strength training is enough.

One kind of app this guide leaves out: follow-along video classes, such as Nike Training Club, Apple Fitness+ and Peloton.

Questions people ask before picking one

Is there a free app for following a workout program?

Yes. Boostcamp's free tier includes 99 of its 132 coach-made programs, plus a builder for your own. Hevy's free plan logs unlimited workouts with up to 4 routines, and Strong's free version keeps 3. A spreadsheet is free too, and for some people it's the right tool: here's when a spreadsheet beats an app. {{kiron:free-tier-sentence}}

Is there a workout plan app without a subscription?

Two of the apps here sell a one-time upgrade: Hevy Pro for $74.99 and Strong Pro for $99.99. The rest are subscriptions: StrongLifts sells plans of up to five years, Fitbod, Ladder and Runna are monthly or yearly, and Kiron is {{kiron:price-monthly}} or {{kiron:price-annual}}.

Which workout planner apps work with Apple Watch?

Hevy, Strong, Fitbod, StrongLifts, Ladder and Runna have Apple Watch apps, and Runna also sends runs to Garmin and COROS watches. On Android watches (Wear OS), Hevy and Fitbod have apps. Boostcamp and Kiron have no Watch app; Kiron reads heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect after a workout.

Can I put a coach's or ChatGPT's plan into an app?

In most apps you rebuild it by hand, one routine or saved workout at a time. Boostcamp's web builder can import a spreadsheet, and Hevy's ChatGPT app can create a plan in Hevy. Kiron reads the plan you already have, pasted as text or from a photo, and turns it into a program, including plans that change every few weeks.

What app handles running and lifting together?

If the race comes first, Runna, with its strength sessions as support work. If you want a full lifting program and your runs in one plan, Kiron plans both, with programs like Run + Lift and Sprint Triathlon. Our post on running and lifting in the same week covers how to space the hard days.

If you'd like a plan run for you, whether it's one of Kiron's {{kiron:program-count}} programs or the one you're following now, try Kiron. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron.

If you only need to log a routine you know by heart, start with Hevy or Strong. For a big library of coach-made programs, look at Boostcamp.
